name: Pageboy

card.summary: A smooth chin-length cut with ends turned under and often a straight fringe, giving a sleek, symmetrical frame around the face.
card.note: Suits straight to slightly wavy hair best; the under-turned finish needs regular styling.

quick.overview:
The pageboy is a women's hairstyle of straight, even-length hair at or near chin length with the ends rolled under, frequently with a straight fringe. The result is a rounded, polished outline.

It frames the face symmetrically and puts emphasis on the eyes and cheekbones. Revivals in the 1960s, 1990s and the 2020s 'pageboy bob' keep it in circulation.
quick.how: Stylists cut the hair to a uniform length and set the ends under with a round brush and blow-dryer, hot rollers or a curling iron. Straight and slightly wavy textures hold the shape most easily.
quick.risks: Heat styling used to turn the ends can dry hair, and the blunt line needs frequent trims to keep its shape. No health issues are specific to the cut.

lead: The pageboy is a hairstyle of straight hair cut to about chin or shoulder length with the ends turned under and, often, straight bangs, giving a geometric, bowl-like silhouette.[1] The name is linked to the simple cuts attributed to young male attendants in medieval English courts.[1]
It is distinct from the standard bob, whose ends are straight or flipped out, because the pageboy curls inward.[1] Wikipedia lists it among bob-related styles, usually a bit longer than a bob.[2]
The bob in general was revived in the mid-1960s by Vidal Sassoon alongside the Beatles' mop-top, and returned again in the 2000s.[2] Grokipedia lists a 2020s resurgence as the 'pageboy bob'.[1]

chain: Uniform chin-length cut with ends tucked under
Smooth, symmetrical outline around the face
angle.text: The cut changes the outline around the face and, with a fringe, focuses attention on the eyes. It works through shape and sleekness.

infobox: Ends rolled under, often straight fringe

paras: Hair is cut to an even length around the head and the ends are turned under for a rounded finish.[1] A straight fringe adds to the structured look.[1]
Stylists describe setting the ends with hot rollers, curling irons or pin curls, or blow-drying with a round brush, then smoothing with a soft brush.[1]

Short women's hair gained acceptance around the First World War era, and bobs dominated the mid-1920s before sharp lines faded in the 1930s.[2] The pageboy's revivals followed the 1960s bob and Beatles-era cuts, then the 1990s, where Uma Thurman's character in Pulp Fiction is a widely cited example.[1][2]

timeline.event: Vidal Sassoon revives the bob; the Beatles' mop-top is popular.[2]
Pulp Fiction's Mia Wallace is cited as a pop-culture reference for the style.[1]
